parts: Tourism moves people, so it needs transport, accommodation, food and guides, and it brings tourists into contact with the local land and people. The impacts are grouped as economic, socio-cultural, political and environmental, and each has a positive and a negative side. India's variety of landscape, climate, monuments, religious places and adventure sites favours tourism: south India is sought in winter and the Himalayas in summer.

Positive: income and growth of allied sectors; foreign exchange (helps the balance of trade); government revenue from taxes, entry fees, tolls and import duty; jobs for guides, hotel staff, taxi drivers and craftspeople; investment in infrastructure; livelihood in the informal sector (street vendors, rickshaw pullers, tea stalls) that pumps money into the local economy.

Negative: hidden costs and leakage of profit to richer countries (goods are imported, and in all-inclusive packages about two-thirds of the spending goes to airlines, hotels and international companies); price rises that hurt local people; higher land and service costs; seasonal, insecure jobs; displacement of people for airports, resorts and reserves.

Culture covers manners, morals, beliefs, behaviour, values and norms. Positive: meeting people of other cultures, education and cultural exchange, less prejudice and tension, better community facilities, pride in heritage, demand for local arts and crafts as souvenirs, and festivals kept alive.

Negative: weaker family bonds and more nuclear families, urbanisation and emigration, friction over overcrowding, drug abuse and prostitution, exploitation of children and young women, commercialisation of traditional welcome, loss of cultural identity, crime from greed, youth imitating tourists (smoking, drinking, gambling), tourists breaking local norms, erosion of local language, cultural clashes and a widening gap between haves and have-nots.

Politics affects tourism more than tourism affects politics. A tourism policy is a set of rules, guidelines and directives for developing and promoting tourism. Positive: political stability, law and order, protection of tourists, political will to build infrastructure, tourist-targeted planning, beautification without altering the landscape. Negative: political instability and conflict, travel advisories and warnings from tourists' home governments, terrorism, naxal activity and communal conflict (the unrest in the Kashmir valley reduced tourism), and an unfavourable policy. Risk perception influences where tourists choose to go.

Negative: change in land use, loss of forest and farmland, soil erosion, landslides and floods on mountain slopes, loss of biodiversity, depletion and pollution of water, air and land, pollution of beaches, lakes and rivers, congestion, solid waste and sewage, emissions from flights and local transport, damage to heritage sites, pressure on fragile mountain areas, litter on trekking paths, disturbance of animals in parks and sanctuaries, trampling of vegetation and visual clutter from tall buildings.

Positive: environmental awareness, funds for conservation and beautification, cleanliness drives, protective measures, ecological balance as an objective, research on the effects of tourism, awareness among local people, protection of monuments and museums, parks and gardens, and the renovation of buildings and reuse of degraded land.

Sustainable tourism keeps resources and local features available for all time and does not degrade the environment. It balances economic, socio-cultural and environmental factors (three tridents; four pillars if society is split into social and cultural). Tourist carrying capacity (UNWTO) is the maximum number of people who can visit a destination at the same time without harming its physical, economic and socio-cultural environment or the quality of life.

India's tourism policy follows the 7-S mantras: Swagat (welcome), Soochanaa (information), Suvidha (facilitation), Suraksha (security), Sahyog (cooperation), Sanrachnaa (infrastructure) and Safai (cleanliness).
